claim: Cut-and-paste DNA transposons of the mariner/Tc1 family are useful tools for genome engineering.
source: Cut-and-paste DNA transposons of the mariner/Tc1 family are useful tools for genome engineering and are inserted specifically at TA target sites.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of mariner/Tc1 transposons, supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Mariner/Tc1 transposons are inserted specifically at TA target sites.
source: Cut-and-paste DNA transposons of the mariner/Tc1 family are useful tools for genome engineering and are inserted specifically at TA target sites.
evidence: This is a well-established characteristic of mariner/Tc1 transposons, supported by prior knowledge and citations in the manuscript.

claim: A crystal structure of the mariner transposase Mos1 in complex with transposon ends covalently joined to target DNA portrays the transposition machinery after DNA integration.
source: A crystal structure of the mariner transposase Mos1 (derived from Drosophila mauritiana), in complex with transposon ends covalently joined to target DNA, portrays the transposition machinery after DNA integration.
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystallographic data presented in the manuscript, including structure determination and refinement statistics.

claim: The Mos1 STC structure reveals severe distortion of target DNA.
source: It reveals severe distortion of target DNA and flipping of the target adenines into extra-helical positions.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Mos1 STC structure reveals flipping of the target adenines into extra-helical positions.
source: It reveals severe distortion of target DNA and flipping of the target adenines into extra-helical positions.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure and confirmed by fluorescence experiments.

claim: Fluorescence experiments confirm dynamic base flipping in solution.
source: Fluorescence experiments confirm dynamic base flipping in solution.
evidence: This is supported by time-resolved fluorescence spectroscopy data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Transposase residues W159, R186, F187 and K190 stabilise the target DNA distortions.
source: Transposase residues W159, R186, F187 and K190 stabilise the target DNA distortions and are required for efficient transposon integration and transposition in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and mutagenesis experiments showing reduced activity with alanine substitutions.

claim: Transposase residues W159, R186, F187 and K190 are required for efficient transposon integration and transposition in vitro.
source: Transposase residues W159, R186, F187 and K190 stabilise the target DNA distortions and are required for efficient transposon integration and transposition in vitro.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro strand transfer and transposition assays with mutant transposases.

claim: Transposase recognises the flipped target adenines via base-specific interactions with backbone atoms.
source: Transposase recognises the flipped target adenines via base-specific interactions with backbone atoms, offering a molecular basis for TA target sequence selection.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure showing hydrogen bonds between adenine and V214 backbone atoms.

claim: Base-specific interactions between transposase and flipped adenines offer a molecular basis for TA target sequence selection.
source: Transposase recognises the flipped target adenines via base-specific interactions with backbone atoms, offering a molecular basis for TA target sequence selection.
evidence: This is inferred from structural observations and supported by experiments with adenine analogues.

claim: Transposable elements are ubiquitous in most genomes and promote evolution by generating genetic diversity.
source: Transposable elements are ubiquitous in most genomes and promote evolution by generating genetic diversity (Biémont and Vieira, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Domestication of a Transib-type DNA transposon led to V(D)J recombination and adaptive immunity in jawed vertebrates.
source: For example, domestication of a Transib-type DNA transposon led to V(D)J recombination and adaptive immunity in jawed vertebrates (Kapitonov and Jurka, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The Cas1 integrase component of prokaryotic CRISPR-Cas systems of adaptive immunity originated from DNA transposons named Casposons.
source: Similarly, the Cas1 integrase component of prokaryotic CRISPR-Cas systems of adaptive immunity originated from DNA transposons named Casposons (Krupovic et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Integration of spacer sequences into the CRISPR locus by the Cas1-Cas2 complex has similarities with transposon and retroviral DNA integration.
source: Integration of spacer sequences into the CRISPR locus by the Cas1-Cas2 complex has similarities with transposon and retroviral DNA integration (Nuñez et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Many DNA transposases share a conserved RNase H-like catalytic domain with retroviral integrases and RAG recombinases.
source: Many DNA transposases (e.g. Mos1, Tn5 and bacteriophage MuA) share a conserved RNase H-like catalytic domain, along with retroviral integrases (e.g. HIV-1) and RAG recombinases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the structural similarity of these enzymes.

claim: DDE/D enzymes use common active site chemistry to perform similar DNA cleavage and DNA integration reactions.
source: These DDE/D enzymes use common active site chemistry to perform similar DNA cleavage and DNA integration reactions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the catalytic mechanism of DDE/D enzymes.

claim: Most DDE/D recombinases show only limited preference for a consensus target DNA sequence, which is usually palindromic.
source: Most DDE/D recombinases show only limited preference for a consensus target DNA sequence, which is usually palindromic (Goryshin et al., 1998; Halling and Kleckner, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Some retroviral integrases preferentially insert their viral genome into nucleosomal DNA.
source: Some retroviral integrases (e.g. prototype foamy virus (PFV) and HIV-1) preferentially insert their viral genome into nucleosomal DNA (Pruss et al., 1994; Maskell et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Some transposases favour bent target DNA structures.
source: Similarly, some transposases (e.g. Tn10) favour bent target DNA structures (Pribil and Haniford, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Mariner/Tc1/IS630 family transposases integrate their transposons, with a 2 bp stagger, strictly at TA target sequences.
source: Mariner/Tc1/IS630 family transposases are unusual as they integrate their transposons, with a 2 bp stagger, strictly at TA target sequences (Tellier et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The reconstructed Tc1 transposase Sleeping Beauty is being used in human clinical trials to treat B-cell lymphoma by genetic engineering of T cells.
source: For example, the reconstructed Tc1 transposase Sleeping Beauty (Ivics et al., 1997) is being used in human clinical trials to treat B-cell lymphoma by genetic engineering of T cells (Maiti et al., 2013) and in pre-clinical studies to reduce age-related macular degeneration (Johnen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Sleeping Beauty is being used in pre-clinical studies to reduce age-related macular degeneration.
source: For example, the reconstructed Tc1 transposase Sleeping Beauty (Ivics et al., 1997) is being used in human clinical trials to treat B-cell lymphoma by genetic engineering of T cells (Maiti et al., 2013) and in pre-clinical studies to reduce age-related macular degeneration (Johnen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Up to 45 kb of DNA can be inserted into the C. elegans genome using a transposition system engineered from the mariner transposon Mos1 from Drosophila mauritiana.
source: Up to 45 kb of DNA can be inserted into the C. elegans genome using a transposition system engineered from the mariner transposon Mos1 from Drosophila mauritiana (Frøkjær-Jensen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The 1286 bp Mos1 transposon is framed by 28 bp imperfect inverted repeats.
source: The 1286 bp transposon is framed by 28 bp imperfect inverted repeats (IR) (Jacobson et al., 1986) and encodes a 345 amino acid transposase that can perform cut-and-paste DNA transposition in vitro (Lampe et al., 1996), as shown in Figure 1a.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The Mos1 transposon encodes a 345 amino acid transposase that can perform cut-and-paste DNA transposition in vitro.
source: The 1286 bp transposon is framed by 28 bp imperfect inverted repeats (IR) (Jacobson et al., 1986) and encodes a 345 amino acid transposase that can perform cut-and-paste DNA transposition in vitro (Lampe et al., 1996), as shown in Figure 1a.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The Mos1 transposase homodimer binds to the IR at one transposon end.
source: The Mos1 transposase homodimer binds to the IR at one transposon end (Cuypers et al., 2013) and then captures the other IR, forming a paired-end complex (PEC).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The Mos1 transposase captures the other IR after binding to one transposon end, forming a paired-end complex (PEC).
source: The Mos1 transposase homodimer binds to the IR at one transposon end (Cuypers et al., 2013) and then captures the other IR, forming a paired-end complex (PEC).
evidence: This is inferred from the cited work and the description of the transposition pathway.

claim: The trans architecture of the PEC regulates coordinated excision of the transposon ends.
source: The trans architecture of the PEC regulates coordinated excision of the transposon ends (Richardson et al., 2009) and cross-talk between transposase sub-units (Bouuaert et al., 2014; Dornan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The trans architecture of the PEC regulates cross-talk between transposase sub-units.
source: The trans architecture of the PEC regulates coordinated excision of the transposon ends (Richardson et al., 2009) and cross-talk between transposase sub-units (Bouuaert et al., 2014; Dornan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: After excision, the Mos1 transpososome locates a TA target integration site.
source: After excision, the Mos1 transpososome locates a TA target integration site (Pflieger et al., 2014) and, upon binding, forms a target capture complex (TCC) (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Upon binding to a TA target site, the Mos1 transpososome forms a target capture complex (TCC).
source: After excision, the Mos1 transpososome locates a TA target integration site (Pflieger et al., 2014) and, upon binding, forms a target capture complex (TCC) (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is inferred from the description of the transposition pathway and supported by the cited work.

claim: Mos1 STC crystals diffracted X-rays to a maximum resolution of 3.3 Å.
source: Mos1 STC crystals diffracted X-rays to a maximum resolution of 3.3 Å.
evidence: This is directly stated in the manuscript and supported by the crystallographic data.

claim: The crystallographic asymmetric unit contains one Mos1 STC.
source: The crystallographic asymmetric unit contains one Mos1 STC and, as predicted, base pairing of the 4 nt overhangs in adjacent complexes facilitates crystal packing (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is directly stated in the manuscript and supported by the crystallographic data.

claim: Base pairing of the 4 nt overhangs in adjacent complexes facilitates crystal packing.
source: The crystallographic asymmetric unit contains one Mos1 STC and, as predicted, base pairing of the 4 nt overhangs in adjacent complexes facilitates crystal packing (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The refined Mos1 STC model has an R(free) of 27.9% and good stereochemistry.
source: The refined model has an R(free) of 27.9% and good stereochemistry.
evidence: This is directly stated in the manuscript and supported by the refinement statistics in Table 2.

claim: The refined Mos1 STC crystal structure contains a transposase homodimer bound to two DNA duplexes representing the products of transposon integration.
source: The refined Mos1 STC crystal structure (Figure 2a) contains a transposase homodimer bound to two DNA duplexes representing the products of transposon integration.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Target DNA binds in a channel between the two catalytic domains in the Mos1 STC.
source: Target DNA binds in a channel between the two catalytic domains and the active sites contain the strand transfer products.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The active sites of the Mos1 STC contain the strand transfer products.
source: Target DNA binds in a channel between the two catalytic domains and the active sites contain the strand transfer products.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The TCC contains a transposase dimer.
source: As the TCC also contains a transposase dimer (Pflieger et al., 2014), our new STC structure indicates that Mos1 strand transfer, like transposon excision, is catalysed by a transposase dimer.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Mos1 strand transfer is catalysed by a transposase dimer.
source: As the TCC also contains a transposase dimer (Pflieger et al., 2014), our new STC structure indicates that Mos1 strand transfer, like transposon excision, is catalysed by a transposase dimer.
evidence: This is inferred from the STC structure showing a dimer and the cited work on the TCC.

claim: The transposase subunits adopt a crossed (or trans) arrangement with IR DNA in the Mos1 STC.
source: The transposase subunits adopt a crossed (or trans) arrangement with IR DNA in the Mos1 STC, similar to the pre- and post-TS cleavage Mos1 PECs (Dornan et al., 2015; Richardson et al., 2009): each IR is recognised by the DNA-binding domain of one transposase subunit and by the catalytic domain of the other subunit (Figure 2b), and vice versa.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure and shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The trans arrangement of transposase subunits brings the cleaved transposon ends together.
source: This brings the cleaved transposon ends together, and ensures suitable spacing for their integration into TA target DNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural arrangement observed in the STC.

claim: The trans arrangement of transposase subunits ensures suitable spacing for integration into TA target DNA.
source: This brings the cleaved transposon ends together, and ensures suitable spacing for their integration into TA target DNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural arrangement observed in the STC.

claim: Transposase interactions with IR DNA in the STC are similar to those in the post-TS cleavage PEC.
source: Transposase interactions with IR DNA in the STC (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) are similar to those in the post-TS cleavage PEC, suggesting that, after transposon excision, the transpososome is poised for target capture.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the STC structure with the post-TS cleavage PEC structure.

claim: After transposon excision, the transpososome is poised for target capture.
source: Transposase interactions with IR DNA in the STC (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) are similar to those in the post-TS cleavage PEC, suggesting that, after transposon excision, the transpososome is poised for target capture.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of transposase-IR DNA interactions in the STC and post-TS cleavage PEC.

claim: Target DNA is deformed rather than the transposase and IR DNA being rearranged during target capture.
source: Thus, rather than rearrange the transposase and IR DNA, target DNA is deformed to enable strand transfer.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural comparison of the STC with the PECs.

claim: The target DNA backbone is bent by 147° in the Mos1 STC.
source: The target DNA is severely distorted from B-form conformation (Figure 2c): the backbone is bent by 147°, with the apex of the bend at the TA target dinucleotide.
evidence: This is directly measured from the crystal structure shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The apex of the target DNA bend is at the TA target dinucleotide.
source: The target DNA is severely distorted from B-form conformation (Figure 2c): the backbone is bent by 147°, with the apex of the bend at the TA target dinucleotide.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: DNA unwinds most readily at TA sequences due to the inherent bendability of a pyrimidine-purine step and the lower stability of a TA base pair.
source: DNA unwinds most readily at TA sequences due to the inherent bendability of a pyrimidine-purine step (which has minimal base-to-base overlap and low twist angles) and the lower stability of a TA base pair, compared to CG.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DNA structure and stability.

claim: The strand transfer reaction creates a nick in both target DNA strands 5' of the target thymine T0.
source: The strand transfer reaction creates a nick in both target DNA strands 5' of the target thymine T0, which likely relieves steric constraints and allows the extreme bend across the TA di-nucleotide.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure and is a consequence of the strand transfer reaction mechanism.

claim: The nick created by strand transfer likely relieves steric constraints and allows the extreme bend across the TA di-nucleotide.
source: The strand transfer reaction creates a nick in both target DNA strands 5' of the target thymine T0, which likely relieves steric constraints and allows the extreme bend across the TA di-nucleotide.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observation of the bent DNA and the nick.

claim: Each Mos1 transposase active site comprises the carboxylate side-chains of three conserved aspartates (D156, D249 and D284) from the same catalytic domain.
source: Each Mos1 transposase active site comprises the carboxylate side-chains of three conserved aspartates (D156, D249 and D284) from the same catalytic domain, which coordinate the metal ions (Mg2+ or Mn2+) required for catalysis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Mos1 active site and is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The active site aspartates coordinate the metal ions (Mg2+ or Mn2+) required for catalysis.
source: Each Mos1 transposase active site comprises the carboxylate side-chains of three conserved aspartates (D156, D249 and D284) from the same catalytic domain, which coordinate the metal ions (Mg2+ or Mn2+) required for catalysis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DDE/D enzymes and is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: One Mg2+ was observed in each active site in the Mos1 STC.
source: One Mg2+ was observed in each active site in the Mos1 STC, coordinated by the D156 and D249 carboxylates, the 3'-OH of C-1 and a water molecule.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The Mg2+ in each active site is coordinated by the D156 and D249 carboxylates, the 3'-OH of C-1 and a water molecule.
source: One Mg2+ was observed in each active site in the Mos1 STC, coordinated by the D156 and D249 carboxylates, the 3'-OH of C-1 and a water molecule.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The phosphodiester joining each transposon 3' end (A56) to a T0 passes close to an active site.
source: The phosphodiester joining each transposon 3' end (A56) to a T0 passes close to an active site (Figure 2b,c,d).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2.

claim: The T0 phosphate oxygens are 4.4 Å and 7 Å from the Mg2+, precluding chelation.
source: The T0 phosphate oxygens are 4.4 Å and 7 Å from the Mg2+, precluding chelation.
evidence: This is directly measured from the crystal structure.

claim: The C-1 3'-OH is not in-line with the T0–A56 phosphodiester bond.
source: Moreover, the C-1 3'-OH is not in-line with the T0–A56 phosphodiester bond, consistent with repositioning of the nascent transposon-target DNA junction, away from the active site Mg2+ after strand transfer.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The nascent transposon-target DNA junction is repositioned away from the active site Mg2+ after strand transfer.
source: Moreover, the C-1 3'-OH is not in-line with the T0–A56 phosphodiester bond, consistent with repositioning of the nascent transposon-target DNA junction, away from the active site Mg2+ after strand transfer.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observation that the C-1 3'-OH is not in-line with the T0–A56 phosphodiester bond.

claim: Repositioning of the transposon-target DNA junction away from the active site likely prevents self-destructive disintegration and drives transposition forwards.
source: Similar to the PFV STC (Maertens et al., 2010), this likely prevents self-destructive disintegration and drives transposition forwards.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observation and comparison with the PFV STC.

claim: Each transposon–target thymine junction is clearly defined in the electron density map.
source: Each transposon–target thymine junction is clearly defined in the electron density map (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is directly observed in the electron density map shown in Figure 2d.

claim: There is clear density for the nucleobase of T0 on strand b (magenta) in active site B.
source: There is also clear density for the nucleobase of T0 on strand b (magenta) in active site B.
evidence: This is directly observed in the electron density map.

claim: No clear density was observed for the T0 base on strand t (active site A), indicating some disorder in its position.
source: However, we observed no clear density for the T0 base on strand t (active site A), indicating some disorder in its position.
evidence: This is directly observed in the electron density map.

claim: In active site B the T0 nucleobase π–π stacks with the base of C-1.
source: In active site B the T0 nucleobase π–π stacks with the base of C-1 to which T0 would have been connected before strand transfer.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The T0 base is unpaired in the Mos1 STC.
source: The T0 base is unpaired and O4 is 3.4 Å from the H122 imidazole NH, suggesting a possible base-specific hydrogen bond (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 3a.

claim: T0 O4 is 3.4 Å from the H122 imidazole NH, suggesting a possible base-specific hydrogen bond.
source: The T0 base is unpaired and O4 is 3.4 Å from the H122 imidazole NH, suggesting a possible base-specific hydrogen bond (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is directly measured from the crystal structure and represents a hypothesis about a potential interaction.

claim: The mutation H122A had no effect on the strand transfer efficiency.
source: However, the mutation H122A had no effect on the strand transfer efficiency (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and we conclude that the putative thymine-specific hydrogen bond is not required for target integration and may be transient, due to T0 base mobility.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro strand transfer assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The putative thymine-specific hydrogen bond between T0 and H122 is not required for target integration.
source: However, the mutation H122A had no effect on the strand transfer efficiency (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and we conclude that the putative thymine-specific hydrogen bond is not required for target integration and may be transient, due to T0 base mobility.
evidence: This is concluded from the mutagenesis experiment showing no effect of H122A on strand transfer.

claim: The putative thymine-specific hydrogen bond may be transient, due to T0 base mobility.
source: However, the mutation H122A had no effect on the strand transfer efficiency (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and we conclude that the putative thymine-specific hydrogen bond is not required for target integration and may be transient, due to T0 base mobility.
evidence: This is speculated based on the lack of effect of the H122A mutation and the disorder observed for T0 in active site A.

claim: Both target adenine (A1) bases of the symmetrical TA sequence are flipped into extra-helical positions in the Mos1 STC.
source: The most striking feature of the Mos1 STC structure is flipping of both target adenine (A1) bases of the symmetrical TA sequence into extra-helical positions (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The phosphate backbone atoms of A1 and G2 are rotated by ~180°, with respect to the adjacent nucleotides.
source: The phosphate backbone atoms of A1 and G2 are rotated by ~180°, with respect to the adjacent nucleotides, so that the A1 bases cannot pair with their complementary T0.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The A1 bases cannot pair with their complementary T0 due to the backbone rotation.
source: The phosphate backbone atoms of A1 and G2 are rotated by ~180°, with respect to the adjacent nucleotides, so that the A1 bases cannot pair with their complementary T0.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: Each unpaired A1 is wedged against the ribose face of the complementary target strand, at an oblique angle to bases G2 and C3.
source: Instead each unpaired A1 is wedged against the ribose face of the complementary target strand, at an oblique angle to bases G2 and C3 (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The aromatic ring of each F187 occupies the space vacated by a flipped A1.
source: The aromatic ring of each F187 occupies the space vacated by a flipped A1, forming a π–π stack with the adjacent G2 nucleobase, stabilising this conformation (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 3a.

claim: F187 forms a π–π stack with the adjacent G2 nucleobase, stabilising the flipped A1 conformation.
source: The aromatic ring of each F187 occupies the space vacated by a flipped A1, forming a π–π stack with the adjacent G2 nucleobase, stabilising this conformation (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure and represents a structural interpretation of the stabilizing interaction.

claim: Upon addition of Mos1 transposase to TA1, complete formation of a nucleoprotein complex was observed by gel-filtration chromatography.
source: Upon addition of Mos1 transposase to TA1, we observed complete formation of a nucleoprotein complex by gel-filtration chromatography (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gel-filtration chromatography data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: When Mos1 transposase was added to TP13, there was no measurable change in the steady-state fluorescence intensity at 367 nm.
source: When Mos1 transposase was added to TP13, there was no measurable change in the (very low) steady-state fluorescence intensity at 367 nm (inset, Figure 3c), consistent with no change in the 2AP environment upon STC formation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the steady-state fluorescence data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The lack of change in fluorescence intensity for TP13 upon transposase addition is consistent with no change in the 2AP environment upon STC formation.
source: When Mos1 transposase was added to TP13, there was no measurable change in the (very low) steady-state fluorescence intensity at 367 nm (inset, Figure 3c), consistent with no change in the 2AP environment upon STC formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the fluorescence data, which shows no change when 2AP is in a stacked, base-paired position.

claim: There was a ten fold increase in fluorescence intensity when Mos1 transposase was added to TP1.
source: In contrast, there was a ten fold increase in fluorescence intensity when Mos1 transposase was added to TP1 (inset, Figure 3d), consistent with 2AP at the target site becoming unstacked by flipping into an unquenched, extra-helical environment in the Mos1 STC.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the steady-state fluorescence data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The ten fold increase in fluorescence intensity for TP1 upon transposase addition is consistent with 2AP at the target site becoming unstacked by flipping into an unquenched, extra-helical environment.
source: In contrast, there was a ten fold increase in fluorescence intensity when Mos1 transposase was added to TP1 (inset, Figure 3d), consistent with 2AP at the target site becoming unstacked by flipping into an unquenched, extra-helical environment in the Mos1 STC.
evidence: This is inferred from the fluorescence data, which shows a large increase when 2AP is at the target adenine position.

claim: In the absence of transposase, 90% of the 2AP population of TP13 has the shortest lifetime (τ1=30ps), indicating a tightly stacked duplex structure.
source: In the absence of transposase, 90% of the 2AP population of TP13 has the shortest lifetime (τ1=30ps), indicating a tightly stacked duplex structure.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the time-resolved fluorescence data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Upon addition of Mos1 transposase to TP13, the decay parameters are essentially unchanged.
source: Upon addition of Mos1 transposase, the decay parameters are essentially unchanged showing that the local duplex structure is unaffected, confirming the steady-state fluorescence results.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the time-resolved fluorescence data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: TP1 fluorescence decay, in the absence of protein, is dominated by the shortest lifetime, stacked component (76%, τ1= 50 ps).
source: TP1 fluorescence decay, in the absence of protein, is also dominated by the shortest lifetime, stacked component (76%, τ1= 50 ps, Figure 3d), with only 6% of the population in the unstacked state (τ4 = 7.5 ns).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the time-resolved fluorescence data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: In the absence of protein, only 6% of the TP1 population is in the unstacked state (τ4 = 7.5 ns).
source: TP1 fluorescence decay, in the absence of protein, is also dominated by the shortest lifetime, stacked component (76%, τ1= 50 ps, Figure 3d), with only 6% of the population in the unstacked state (τ4 = 7.5 ns).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the time-resolved fluorescence data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Upon addition of transposase to TP1, there is a large transfer of population from the highly stacked state (τ1 = 80 ps) to the unstacked, unquenched state (τ4 9.7 ns).
source: However, upon addition of transposase to TP1, the decay parameters change markedly (Figure 3d). Most notably, there is a large transfer of population from the highly stacked state (τ1 = 80 ps) to the unstacked, unquenched state (τ4 9.7 ns); the population of the former falls to 38% and that of the latter increases concomitantly to 31%.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the time-resolved fluorescence data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Upon addition of transposase to TP1, the population of the highly stacked state falls to 38% and that of the unstacked state increases to 31%.
source: However, upon addition of transposase to TP1, the decay parameters change markedly (Figure 3d). Most notably, there is a large transfer of population from the highly stacked state (τ1 = 80 ps) to the unstacked, unquenched state (τ4 9.7 ns); the population of the former falls to 38% and that of the latter increases concomitantly to 31%.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the time-resolved fluorescence data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: In solution, 2AP at the position of the target adenine A1 in the Mos1 STC experiences base-flipping into an extra-helical environment.
source: This clearly confirms that, in solution, 2AP at the position of the target adenine A1 in the Mos1 STC experiences base-flipping into an extra-helical environment.
evidence: This is concluded from the time-resolved fluorescence data showing a large increase in the unstacked population.

claim: Flipping of 2AP at the target adenine position is dynamic: a number of conformational states are sampled, including base-flipped and base-stacked environments.
source: Moreover, flipping of this 2AP is dynamic: a number of conformational states are sampled, including base-flipped and base-stacked environments.
evidence: This is concluded from the time-resolved fluorescence data showing multiple lifetime components.

claim: Side-chain atoms of transposase residues R186, K190 and W159 stabilise the distortions caused by base flipping of each A1.
source: Base flipping of each A1 severely distorts the surrounding target DNA. Side-chain atoms of transposase residues R186, K190 and W159 stabilise these distortions (Figure 4a) by forming salt bridges or hydrogen bonds with the A1 and G2 phosphates.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 4a.

claim: R186, K190 and W159 stabilise target DNA distortions by forming salt bridges or hydrogen bonds with the A1 and G2 phosphates.
source: Base flipping of each A1 severely distorts the surrounding target DNA. Side-chain atoms of transposase residues R186, K190 and W159 stabilise these distortions (Figure 4a) by forming salt bridges or hydrogen bonds with the A1 and G2 phosphates.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The DNA backbone rotations bring the G2 phosphates on both target DNA strands within 6.7 Å of each other.
source: The DNA backbone rotations bring the G2 phosphates on both target DNA strands within 6.7 Å of each other and close to the guanidinium group of R186 in subunit A (R186A); each NηH2 group hydrogen bonds with a G2 phosphate oxygen on one strand (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is directly measured from the crystal structure shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Each NηH2 group of R186A hydrogen bonds with a G2 phosphate oxygen on one strand.
source: The DNA backbone rotations bring the G2 phosphates on both target DNA strands within 6.7 Å of each other and close to the guanidinium group of R186 in subunit A (R186A); each NηH2 group hydrogen bonds with a G2 phosphate oxygen on one strand (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The K190 side-chain NζH2 forms a salt bridge with the other G2 phosphate oxygen on one strand.
source: In both subunits, the K190 side-chain NζH2 forms a salt bridge with the other G2 phosphate oxygen on one strand.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The W159 indole N1H interacts with an A1 phosphate oxygen.
source: Furthermore, the W159 indole N1H interacts with an A1 phosphate oxygen.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The NηH2 group of R186B interacts with the other A1 phosphate oxygen on the top strand.
source: Additionally, the NηH2 group of R186B (which has a different conformation to R186A) interacts with the other A1 phosphate oxygen on the top strand (black, Figure 4a).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The NζH2 of K190 is 5.2 Å from the W159 indole ring and forms a cation-π stack.
source: The NζH2 of K190 is 5.2 Å from the W159 indole ring and forms a cation-π stack, further enhancing stability.
evidence: This is directly measured from the crystal structure.

claim: The cation-π stack between K190 and W159 further enhances stability.
source: The NζH2 of K190 is 5.2 Å from the W159 indole ring and forms a cation-π stack, further enhancing stability.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observation of the cation-π interaction.

claim: Individual substitution of W159, R186, F187 or K190 with alanine severely reduced the in vitro strand transfer activity of transposase.
source: Consistent with the structural roles of W159, R186, F187 and K190 in the STC, individual substitution of each of these residues with alanine severely reduced the in vitro strand transfer activity of transposase (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro strand transfer assays shown in Figure 4c,d.

claim: Transposases containing the mutation W159A, R186A, K190A or F187A showed <0.03% integration of fluorescently labelled Mos1 IR DNA into a target DNA duplex.
source: We detected <0.03% integration of fluorescently labelled Mos1 IR DNA into a target DNA duplex with a sole TA, using transposases containing the mutation W159A, R186A, K190A or F187A (Figure 4c,d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro strand transfer assays shown in Figure 4c,d.

claim: The F187W substitution resulted in 9.5% strand transfer, compared to 9.1% with T216A Mos1 transposase.
source: By contrast, the F187W substitution resulted in 9.5% strand transfer, compared to 9.1% with T216A Mos1 transposase.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro strand transfer assays.

claim: An indole ring, like a phenyl ring, can occupy the space vacated by the flipped A1 base and stabilise the strand transfer product by stacking with the G2 base.
source: Thus, an indole ring, like a phenyl ring, can occupy the space vacated by the flipped A1 base and stabilise the strand transfer product by stacking with the G2 base.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that F187W retains strand transfer activity similar to wild-type.

claim: The individual substitutions W159A, K190A or F187A reduced the in vitro transposition efficiency to <20% that of T216A Mos1 transposase.
source: The individual substitutions W159A, K190A or F187A also reduced the in vitro transposition efficiency to <20% that of T216A Mos1 transposase (Figure 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro transposition assays shown in Figure 5.

claim: Transposon excision and concomitant plasmid backbone release was not affected by the transposase mutations R186A, F187A, F187W, K190A, F161A or F161W.
source: Transposon excision, and concomitant plasmid backbone release, was not affected by the transposase mutations R186A, F187A, F187W, K190A, F161A or F161W (Figure 6b,c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by plasmid-based transposon cleavage assays shown in Figure 6b,c.

claim: The W159A mutant transposase excised only 3.9% of the plasmid after 24 hr, compared to 55.6% for the T216A transposase.
source: However, the W159A mutant transposase excised only 3.9% of the plasmid after 24 hr, compared to 55.6% for the T216A transposase.
evidence: This is demonstrated by plasmid-based transposon cleavage assays shown in Figure 6b,c.

claim: Mos1 transposase residues F187, R186 and K190 are required for target DNA integration, but are not essential for earlier cleavage steps.
source: Thus, Mos1 transposase residues F187, R186 and K190 are required for target DNA integration, but are not essential for earlier cleavage steps, whereas W159 is required for both excision and strand transfer.
evidence: This is concluded from the cleavage and strand transfer assays with mutant transposases.

claim: W159 is required for both excision and strand transfer.
source: Thus, Mos1 transposase residues F187, R186 and K190 are required for target DNA integration, but are not essential for earlier cleavage steps, whereas W159 is required for both excision and strand transfer.
evidence: This is concluded from the cleavage and strand transfer assays with the W159A mutant.

claim: K190 and W159 are strictly conserved among mariner transposases.
source: Alignment of the Mos1 transposase sequence, with other mariner and Tc1-like transposases (Figure 7), reveals that K190 and W159, which form a cation-π stack and interact with target DNA phosphates, are strictly conserved among mariner transposases.
evidence: This is observed in the sequence alignment shown in Figure 7.

claim: R186 is not conserved in all mariner transposases.
source: Despite the crucial role of Mos1 R186 for strand transfer in vitro, this residue is not conserved in all mariner transposases.
evidence: This is observed in the sequence alignment shown in Figure 7.

claim: The aromatic nature of F187 is conserved as either F or H in most other mariner transposases.
source: However, the aromatic nature of F187 is conserved as either F or H in most other mariner transposases.
evidence: This is observed in the sequence alignment shown in Figure 7.

claim: Many of the target-stabilising interactions observed in the Mos1 STC may also exist in other mariner transposases.
source: Thus, many of the target-stabilising interactions observed in the Mos1 STC may also exist in other mariner transposases.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of key residues in the sequence alignment.

claim: The Tc1-like sequences have a conserved lysine at the position equivalent to W159 in Mos1.
source: The Tc1-like sequences have a conserved lysine at the position equivalent to W159 in Mos1 and there are two, proximal conserved tryptophans – aligned with Mos1 residues 149 and 194 – which could fulfil the role of W159 in Mos1 (Figure 7).
evidence: This is observed in the sequence alignment shown in Figure 7.

claim: There are two proximal conserved tryptophans in Tc1-like sequences, aligned with Mos1 residues 149 and 194, which could fulfil the role of W159 in Mos1.
source: The Tc1-like sequences have a conserved lysine at the position equivalent to W159 in Mos1 and there are two, proximal conserved tryptophans – aligned with Mos1 residues 149 and 194 – which could fulfil the role of W159 in Mos1 (Figure 7).
evidence: This is observed in the sequence alignment and represents a hypothesis about functional equivalence.

claim: The Tc1-like transposases contain either K or R one amino acid upstream of R186 in Mos1, followed by an aromatic residue: F, H or Y.
source: Furthermore, the Tc1-like transposases contain either K or R one amino acid upstream of R186 in Mos1, followed by an aromatic residue: F, H or Y.
evidence: This is observed in the sequence alignment shown in Figure 7.

claim: These residue pairs in Tc1-like transposases could stabilise target DNA in a similar way to R186 and F187 in Mos1.
source: These residue pairs could stabilise target DNA in a similar way to R186 and F187 in Mos1.
evidence: This is speculated based on the sequence conservation and the structural role of R186 and F187 in Mos1.

claim: There may be common features in the target DNA integration mechanisms of the two branches of the mariner/Tc1 family.
source: Thus, there may be common features in the target DNA integration mechanisms of the two branches of the mariner/Tc1 family.
evidence: This is speculated based on the sequence conservation of key residues.

claim: In the flipped conformation, the Watson-Crick face of each unpaired A1 base makes two adenine-specific hydrogen bonds with V214 backbone atoms.
source: The target-stabilising interactions described above are non-specific. In contrast, in the flipped conformation, the Watson-Crick face of each unpaired A1 base makes two adenine-specific hydrogen bonds with V214 backbone atoms (Figure 8a): the exocyclic 6-amine interacts with the carbonyl oxygen, and N1 interacts with the backbone amide.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 8a.

claim: The exocyclic 6-amine of A1 interacts with the V214 carbonyl oxygen.
source: The target-stabilising interactions described above are non-specific. In contrast, in the flipped conformation, the Watson-Crick face of each unpaired A1 base makes two adenine-specific hydrogen bonds with V214 backbone atoms (Figure 8a): the exocyclic 6-amine interacts with the carbonyl oxygen, and N1 interacts with the backbone amide.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: N1 of A1 interacts with the V214 backbone amide.
source: The target-stabilising interactions described above are non-specific. In contrast, in the flipped conformation, the Watson-Crick face of each unpaired A1 base makes two adenine-specific hydrogen bonds with V214 backbone atoms (Figure 8a): the exocyclic 6-amine interacts with the carbonyl oxygen, and N1 interacts with the backbone amide.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: Replacing each A1 with 2AP resulted in a dramatic loss of specific integration at each T0 5' of the 2AP.
source: We found that replacing both A1s with 2AP (Figure 8c,d) resulted in a dramatic loss of specific integration at each T0 5' of the 2AP, consistent with the predicted loss of adenine-specific hydrogen-bonds with transposase.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro strand transfer assays shown in Figure 8c,d.

claim: The loss of specific integration with 2AP substitution is consistent with the predicted loss of adenine-specific hydrogen-bonds with transposase.
source: We found that replacing both A1s with 2AP (Figure 8c,d) resulted in a dramatic loss of specific integration at each T0 5' of the 2AP, consistent with the predicted loss of adenine-specific hydrogen-bonds with transposase.
evidence: This is inferred from the strand transfer assay results and the structural observation of adenine-specific interactions.

claim: Mos1 integration at TA requires adenine-specific interactions with transposase to trap the flipped A1 conformation.
source: We conclude that Mos1 integration at TA requires adenine-specific interactions with transposase to trap the flipped A1 conformation.
evidence: This is concluded from the strand transfer assays with 2AP-containing target DNA and the fluorescence experiments.

claim: Efficient Mos1 integration occurred at a T0–A1 step when the T0 was base-paired with 2AP.
source: We replaced each A1 individually with 2AP, and efficient Mos1 integration occurred at a T0–A1 step when the T0 was base-pairedwith 2AP, but was reduced at a T0–2AP1 step (Figure 8c,d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro strand transfer assays shown in Figure 8c,d.

claim: Mos1 integration was reduced at a T0–2AP1 step.
source: We replaced each A1 individually with 2AP, and efficient Mos1 integration occurred at a T0–A1 step when the T0 was base-pairedwith 2AP, but was reduced at a T0–2AP1 step (Figure 8c,d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro strand transfer assays shown in Figure 8c,d.

claim: Specific Mos1 integration at a T0 requires trapping of the flipped A1 adjacent to it on the same strand.
source: We conclude that specific Mos1 integration at a T0 requires trapping of the flipped A1 adjacent to it on the same strand.
evidence: This is concluded from the strand transfer assays with individually substituted 2AP.

claim: Only 0.24% integration was measured into the TD sequence.
source: We compared Mos1 strand transfer into TA and the altered target sequences TD and SD, with strengthened and weakened base pairing respectively (Figure 8c, lanes 10 and 11). We measured 6.99% integration into TA, but only 0.24% integration into the TD sequence (Figure 8c,d) and 0.86% integration into SD (Figure 8c); in the latter experiment many other, non-specific integration products were also observed.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro strand transfer assays shown in Figure 8c,d.

claim: 0.86% integration was measured into the SD sequence.
source: We compared Mos1 strand transfer into TA and the altered target sequences TD and SD, with strengthened and weakened base pairing respectively (Figure 8c, lanes 10 and 11). We measured 6.99% integration into TA, but only 0.24% integration into the TD sequence (Figure 8c,d) and 0.86% integration into SD (Figure 8c); in the latter experiment many other, non-specific integration products were also observed.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro strand transfer assays shown in Figure 8c,d.

claim: Many other, non-specific integration products were observed in the SD strand transfer experiment.
source: We compared Mos1 strand transfer into TA and the altered target sequences TD and SD, with strengthened and weakened base pairing respectively (Figure 8c, lanes 10 and 11). We measured 6.99% integration into TA, but only 0.24% integration into the TD sequence (Figure 8c,d) and 0.86% integration into SD (Figure 8c); in the latter experiment many other, non-specific integration products were also observed.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro strand transfer assays shown in Figure 8c.

claim: The weakness of the T:A base pair promotes integration at the TA sequence.
source: Thus, the weakness of the T:A base pair promotes integration at the TA sequence, and the pattern of H-bond donors and acceptors on the Watson-Crick face of adenine is important for specificity.
evidence: This is concluded from the strand transfer assays with TD and SD target sequences.

claim: The pattern of H-bond donors and acceptors on the Watson-Crick face of adenine is important for specificity.
source: Thus, the weakness of the T:A base pair promotes integration at the TA sequence, and the pattern of H-bond donors and acceptors on the Watson-Crick face of adenine is important for specificity.
evidence: This is concluded from the strand transfer assays with 2AP and 2,6-diaminopurine substitutions.

claim: The severe target DNA bend (~147°) is consistent with a bias for mariner/Tc1 integration at highly bendable, palindromic AT-rich sequences.
source: The Mos1 STC structure provides a snapshot of Mos1 transposition in the post-integration state. The severe target DNA bend (~147°) is consistent with a bias for mariner/Tc1 integration at highly bendable, palindromic AT-rich sequences (Vigdal et al., 2002; Yant et al., 2005).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observation of the bent DNA and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Studies by Pflieger et al. suggested that target DNA also bends before Mos1 strand transfer.
source: Studies by Pflieger et al. suggested that target DNA also bends before Mos1 strand transfer (Pflieger et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Comparison of the Mos1 STC structure with the TCC model and both PECs supports the conclusion that target DNA bends before strand transfer.
source: Comparison of the Mos1 STC structure with our previous TCC model (containing straight target DNA) and both the pre- and post-TS cleavage PECs (Dornan et al., 2015; Richardson et al., 2009) supports this conclusion.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural comparison.

claim: The similar architectures and interactions of the IR DNA and transposase in the STC and both PEC structures suggest that target DNA is likely deformed.
source: The similar architectures and interactions of the IR DNA and transposase in the STC and both PEC structures (Figure 9a and Figure 9—figure supplement 1) suggest that target DNA is likely deformed.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural comparison shown in Figure 9a and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Changes to the transposase conformation are subtle and include closing-in of the catalytic domain towards the target DNA after strand transfer.
source: Changes to the transposase conformation are subtle and include closing-in of the catalytic domain towards the target DNA after strand transfer (Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is observed by comparing the STC structure with the PEC structures, as shown in Videos 1 and 2.

claim: The largest displacement in transposase conformation (5.7 Å) is at P210 in the turn between β7 and α8 and around helices α8 and α10.
source: The largest displacement (5.7 Å) is at P210 in the turn between β7 and α8 and around helices α8 and α10, which cradle the target DNA (Figure 9b).
evidence: This is directly measured from the structural comparison shown in Figure 9b.

claim: T0 in the Mos1 STC is in a different orientation to the thymine (T57) of the flanking target site duplication in the pre-TS cleavage PEC.
source: T0 in the Mos1 STC is in a different orientation to the thymine (T57) of the flanking target site duplication in the pre-TS cleavage PEC (Figure 9c), which is recognised by base-specific interactions with the WVPHEL motif (Dornan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is observed by comparing the STC structure with the pre-TS cleavage PEC structure, as shown in Figure 9c.

claim: T0 in the Mos1 STC closely aligns with T54 of the additional DNA duplex in the post-TS cleavage PEC.
source: By contrast, T0 closely aligns with T54 of the additional DNA duplex in the post-TS cleavage PEC (Figure 9d), which may represent the target strand before integration.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the STC structure with the post-TS cleavage PEC structure, as shown in Figure 9d.

claim: T54 of the additional DNA duplex in the post-TS cleavage PEC may represent the target strand before integration.
source: By contrast, T0 closely aligns with T54 of the additional DNA duplex in the post-TS cleavage PEC (Figure 9d), which may represent the target strand before integration.
evidence: This is speculated based on the structural alignment.

claim: Strain created by target DNA bending during target capture likely drives the phosphate backbone rotations that flip the target adenines into extra helical positions.
source: Strain created by target DNA bending during target capture likely drives the phosphate backbone rotations that flip the target adenines into extra helical positions (Figure 10).
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis inferred from the structural observations.

claim: Trapping of the flipped adenines may correctly position the scissile target phosphates for in-line attack by the cleaved transposon ends.
source: Subsequent trapping of the flipped adenines may correctly position the scissile target phosphates for in-line attack by the cleaved transposon ends.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis inferred from the structural observations.

claim: Breaking of the target DNA strands by strand transfer would allow displacement of the new transposon-target DNA junction from the active site, preventing reversal of the reaction.
source: Breaking of the target DNA strands by strand transfer would allow displacement of the new transposon-target DNA junction from the active site, preventing reversal of the reaction.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis inferred from the structural observations.

claim: Many DNA-metabolising enzymes use base flipping to expose bases normally embedded within a double helix.
source: Many DNA-metabolising enzymes use base flipping to expose bases normally embedded within a double helix; enabling base methylation (Klimasauskas et al., 1994), removal of damaged or mismatched bases or for DNA sequence recognition (Bochtler et al., 2006; Neely et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: During Tn5 transposon excision, formation and resolution of DNA hairpins at the transposon ends requires base flipping.
source: During Tn5 transposon excision, formation and resolution of DNA hairpins at the transposon ends requires base flipping: rotation of a base close to the cleavage site, into a protein pocket, relieves strain in the tight hairpin bend and aligns the transposon ends for cleavage (Ason and Reznikoff, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: DNA hairpin stabilisation by base flipping has been proposed for V(D)J recombination and transposition of Hermes and Tn10.
source: Similarly, DNA hairpin stabilisation by base flipping has been proposed for V(D)J recombination and transposition of Hermes and Tn10 (Lu et al., 2006; Bischerour and Chalmers, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: During Mos1 integration, the F187 aromatic ring may actively force the A1s from the DNA helix.
source: During Mos1 integration, the F187 aromatic ring may actively force the A1s from the DNA helix, similar to the methionine probe in Tn10 transposon excision (Bischerour and Chalmers, 2009).
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis based on the structural observation and comparison with Tn10.

claim: F187 may passively fill the gap left by A1 after flipping, to enhance the stability of the distorted target DNA conformation.
source: Alternatively, F187 may passively fill the gap left by A1 after flipping, to enhance the stability of the distorted target DNA conformation.
evidence: This is an alternative mechanistic hypothesis based on the structural observation.

claim: The conserved transposase residues K190 and W159 may be alternative drivers of the base-flipping rotations.
source: In this scenario, the conserved transposase residues K190 and W159 may be alternative drivers of the base-flipping rotations.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis based on the structural observation and sequence conservation.

claim: Target adenine–specific interactions with V214 backbone atoms suggest a molecular basis for TA target sequence recognition in the post-integration state.
source: Target adenine–specific interactions with V214 backbone atoms suggest a molecular basis for TA target sequence recognition in the post-integration state.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observation of adenine-specific interactions.

claim: The structured loop containing V214 has the consensus sequence T-(V/I)-(N/T) in mariner transposases.
source: The structured loop containing V214 has the consensus sequence T-(V/I)-(N/T) in mariner transposases (Figure 7), suggesting that the role of transposase backbone atoms in TA recognition may be conserved among mariner-family transposases.
evidence: This is observed in the sequence alignment shown in Figure 7.

claim: The role of transposase backbone atoms in TA recognition may be conserved among mariner-family transposases.
source: The structured loop containing V214 has the consensus sequence T-(V/I)-(N/T) in mariner transposases (Figure 7), suggesting that the role of transposase backbone atoms in TA recognition may be conserved among mariner-family transposases.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequence conservation.

claim: The Tc1-family transposases also display sequence conservation in the region containing V214.
source: The Tc1-family transposases, including Sleeping Beauty, also display sequence conservation in this region (Figure 7), suggesting similar recognition mechanisms exist in that closely-related family.
evidence: This is observed in the sequence alignment shown in Figure 7.

claim: Similar recognition mechanisms may exist in the Tc1-family transposases.
source: The Tc1-family transposases, including Sleeping Beauty, also display sequence conservation in this region (Figure 7), suggesting similar recognition mechanisms exist in that closely-related family.
evidence: This is speculated based on the sequence conservation.

claim: Target DNA bending is a recurring theme in DNA transposition by DDE/D recombinases.
source: Target DNA bending is a recurring theme in DNA transposition by DDE/D recombinases.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the examples that follow in the manuscript.

claim: The severe target DNA bend (~147°) observed in the Mos1 STC structure is similar to the ~140° target DNA distortion in the bacterial MuA transpososome.
source: The severe target DNA bend (~147°) observed in our Mos1 STC structure is similar to the ~140° target DNA distortion in the bacterial MuA transpososome, which was proposed to drive the isoenergetic strand transfer reaction forward (Montaño et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a comparison with prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: The ~140° target DNA distortion in the bacterial MuA transpososome was proposed to drive the isoenergetic strand transfer reaction forward.
source: The severe target DNA bend (~147°) observed in our Mos1 STC structure is similar to the ~140° target DNA distortion in the bacterial MuA transpososome, which was proposed to drive the isoenergetic strand transfer reaction forward (Montaño et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: MuB may facilitate target DNA bending by forming helical filaments on DNA, prior to capture by the MuA transpososome.
source: Mu employs a helper protein (MuB) in its transposition, which may facilitate target DNA bending by forming helical filaments on DNA, prior to capture by the MuA transpososome (Mizuno et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In the presence of ATP, IstB self-assembles into decamers that can bend ~50 bp DNA by 180°.
source: Similarly, the bacterial insertion sequence IS21 requires IstB for efficient transposition. In the presence of ATP, IstB self-assembles into decamers that can bend ~50 bp DNA by 180° (Arias-Palomo and Berger, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In the PFV integrase target capture and strand transfer complexes, naked target DNA is bent by 55°.
source: In the PFV integrase target capture and strand transfer complexes (Maertens et al., 2010) naked target DNA is bent by 55°.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Nucleosomal DNA is peeled from the histone octamer and similarly deformed by interactions with the PFV intasome.
source: Nucleosomal DNA is peeled from the histone octamer and similarly deformed by interactions with the PFV intasome, providing a structural basis for retroviral integration at nucleosomes (Maskell et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Recent evidence indicates that mariner/Tc1 transposons preferentially integrate at linker regions between nucleosomes.
source: By contrast, recent evidence indicates that mariner/Tc1 transposons preferentially integrate at linker regions between nucleosomes (Gogol-Döring et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Severe target DNA bending (~147°) by the transpososome can be more easily achieved on flexible linker DNA than on DNA tightly engaged with the histone octamer in a nucleosome structure.
source: Our results provide a structural basis for this preference: severe target DNA bending (~147°) by the transpososome can be more easily achieved on flexible linker DNA than on DNA tightly engaged with the histone octamer in a nucleosome structure.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observation of the bent DNA and the cited work on nucleosome preference.

claim: The structural and biochemical data support a dynamic bend, flip and trap mechanism for Mos1 transposon integration at TA target sites.
source: Taken together our structural and biochemical data support a dynamic bend, flip and trap mechanism for Mos1 transposon integration at TA target sites (Figure 10) that may be a conserved feature of mariner/Tc1 transposition.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings and a proposed mechanism based on the data presented.

claim: The bend, flip and trap mechanism may be a conserved feature of mariner/Tc1 transposition.
source: Taken together our structural and biochemical data support a dynamic bend, flip and trap mechanism for Mos1 transposon integration at TA target sites (Figure 10) that may be a conserved feature of mariner/Tc1 transposition.
evidence: This is speculated based on the sequence conservation of key residues.

claim: The results provide a framework for designing mariner/Tc1 transposases with modified target specificities.
source: As such, our results provide a framework for designing mariner/Tc1 transposases with modified target specificities.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential application of the findings.
